thread.title: Barrasso mistaken on Trump, Reagan legacy
thread.title_full: Barrasso mistaken on Trump, Reagan legacy

author: Common Ground / By Paul Hansen
title: Barrasso mistaken on Trump, Reagan legacy
text:
U.S. Sen. John Barrasso’s July 30 “Guest Shot” tried to equate today’s GOP leader, Donald Trump, with President Ronald Reagan. I was in my 30s during the Reagan administration. I remember it well. I respectfully disagree with the senator’s comparison.
Let’s start with the name calling. I did not always agree with Reagan, but he was always humble, dignified and courteous. Not once did he resort to the infantile, bellicose insults Trump levels just about every day. For example, Trump recently called former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi “a disgusting degenerate.”
By comparison, at a retirement party for Democratic Speaker of the House Tip O’Neill in 1986, Reagan said, “Mr. speaker, I’m grateful you have permitted me in the past, and I hope in the future, that singular honor — the honor of calling you my friend.” Or, in his typically avuncular manner, “I would rather go to hell with Tip than heaven without him.”
Here is a link to a YouTube video of Reagan, O’Neill and their spouses laughing hysterically at a juggling comedian: TinyURL.com/MichaelDavisFT. Like many Americans, I long for a return of more civilized political interactions like this.
Sen. Barrasso claims that the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill “means more money in the pockets, purses and paychecks of Wyoming families.” Nice alliteration, senator, but all the independent analysts say this bill gives big tax cuts to the wealthiest, with little benefit to those earning less than $100,000 and no benefit to those earning under $50,000. Much worse for lower-income Wyomingites will be the trillion-dollar cuts to Medicaid and food stamps.
Medicaid fraud is almost entirely committed by Medicaid providers, not Medicaid recipients. Barrasso, a former doctor, must know this. Still, he and today’s GOP have cut IRS enforcement budgets to the bone so IRS cannot go after these criminals. They are not addressing Medicaid fraud; they are cutting access to health care for the poorest Americans.
The senator is wrong on military spending, which has been about 3% of GDP for the last 45 years. He is dishonest when he tells us ICE is arresting “illegal immigrant criminals.” The vast majority of people being arrested are hard working and have no criminal records. They came here at the invitation of American business to do jobs no one wanted. They are a vital part of our economy and community. The senator must know this.
By contrast, Reagan signed the bipartisan Simpson-Mazzoli Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, crafted by our own Sen. Alan Simpson. This was the last immigration reform measure passed by Congress. The act included penalties for employers who hired undocumented workers, amnesty for those here before 1982 who had a job and no criminal record, and increased border enforcement. Congress found common ground. It passed easily.
In February 2024, a similar bipartisan compromise on immigration was killed by Trump’s opposition. Cynically, he did not want the issue resolved so he could use it in his campaign for president.
Barrasso brags about his support for a rescissions bill that saved taxpayers $9 billion. This is .13%, just over one-10th of 1%, of the annual federal budget. He makes no mention of the fact that the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill will increase the national debt by $4 trillion to $5 trillion. Al Simpson is rolling over in his grave at that one.
Remarkably, Barrasso tries to criticize today’s Democrats by pointing to Democrats’ support for Reagan’s 1986 Tax Reform Act. In a stark contrast to today’s Republicans, Reagan again found common ground with Democrats and his friend House Speaker Tip O’Neill to put together bipartisan tax reform. The act got rid of tax loopholes and actually increased revenue. Yes, 30 Senate Democrats voted for it.
Trump and the GOP are not “moving quickly to unleash American energy.” They are opposing it. According to the Texas state comptroller, wind generated 28.6% of Texas electricity — well past coal and nuclear and surpassed only by natural gas at 41.8%. Wind also generated 26,000 Texas jobs, with an average salary of $109,826. We need an “all of the above” energy policy. Like so much else that he does, Trump’s obsessive, obsequious opposition (my alliteration) to wind energy makes no sense.
Today’s GOP leader Donald Trump is no Ronald Reagan.
